13/27.

There are 14 equally likely (sex, birthday-of-week) combinations per child (2 sexes × 7 days), so 196 equally likely outcomes for the pair of children. Among these, the ones satisfying "at least one child is a boy born on Tuesday" are: both children boy-born-Tuesday (1 way), or exactly one child is boy-born-Tuesday and the other is anything else (13 other combinations × 2 orderings = 26 ways), giving 27 outcomes total. Of these 27, the ones where both children are boys consist of: the boy-Tuesday/boy-Tuesday case (1) plus boy-Tuesday paired with one of the other 6 boy/non-Tuesday combinations, in either order (6×2=12), totaling 13. Hence the probability both are boys given the answer "yes" is 13/27 — notably different from the classic 1/3 you get without the birthday detail, since specifying a rare identifying trait (Tuesday) makes it less likely that a random *other* boy in the family coincidentally shares it, tilting the conditional probability toward 1/2.

**Justification.** Each child is one of 2 × 7 = 14 equally likely (sex, weekday) types, so a two-child family has 196 equally likely outcomes. Among the 49 boy–boy weekday combinations, 6 × 6 = 36 contain no Tuesday, leaving 49 − 36 = **13** where both are boys. The answer is therefore 13/27.
